added_claims.claim: Extreme outperformance of alternative markets in 2020-22 raised investors' expectations, so three years of weaker results led to doubts about the thesis even though the earlier gain came from specific sectors; the lower correlation benefit is a long-horizon argument.

added_claims.claim: To avoid over-reading a short period (managers in alternative markets only have about 10 years of data), Quantica measures Sharpe per individual market and adjusts for the period, then reasons from portfolio theory about correlation, instead of judging by which sectors won recently.

corrections.issue: The surprise scenarios are wrong. Katy says the biggest shocks would be a lot more cuts than expected or not enough cuts, that a 50bp cut is what was expected or wanted (so not a surprise), and that getting no cut 'could be huge'.
corrections.fix: With SOFR near 3.4% against fed funds at 4.25-4.5%, rate cuts were priced in, so bond trends need a surprise relative to pricing: a no-cut outcome (or far more cuts than expected) would be the shock, while a 50bp cut is what the market expected; the lack of a trend so far reflects anticipation of the Fed and the jobs data.

corrections.issue: Liberation Day is listed among the observed magnitude surprises, but Katy says it is not in the data set and that she is 'pretty sure' it would be a magnitude surprise.
corrections.fix: In the turbulence paper the large pure magnitude surprises include Brexit, SVB and Black Friday (Liberation Day is outside the sample and only presumed to be one); CTAs do worse on magnitude-surprise days, while correlation surprises mark inflection points where trend signals rotate and drive dispersion.

completeness_estimate: 0.80 - the first reader caught the four dispersion drivers, Man and Quantica findings, turbulence metric and the two-or-three-managers advice, but missed the performance table, fixed-income signal state, the Man hypothetical-manager method, random-signal studies, chance tracking gaps, and several Quantica points (per-market Sharpe, range-bound alt markets, two-edged crowding).
